To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the availability of replicated services can be increased by trading consistency for availability, 2) the maximum availability of a replicated service is bounded by a function of the number of sites, 3) the maximum availability is bounded by a constant that is independent of the communication protocol used to implement consistency, and 4) the maximum availability can be increased by a constant factor by changing from a strict to a non-strict protocol.
i) availability can be improved by dynamically trading consistency for increased availability, and that ii) this can be achieved by simple optimizations to existing protocols.

i) the availability of replicated services is limited by the communication overheads of the underlying consistency protocol, ii) simple optimizations to consistency protocols can significantly improve the availability of replicated systems, and iii) the availability of these services is limited by communication overheads and the number of replicas.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the design of availability-aware replication systems that are able to adapt to changing network conditions.
how to make services more available, not more consistent.
the costs and limits of providing availability for replicated services.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
availability is not a function of consistency alone, but also a function of the consistency protocol and the failure characteristics of the system.
the availability of replicated services is highly sensitive to the consistency level, consistency model, and the failure characteristics of the underlying communication infrastructure.

the availability of a service can be significantly improved through the use of a continuous consistency model and that this availability is limited by the communication costs of the consistency protocol.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the availability of a wide-area replicated service can be increased dramatically by trading off consistency, but that this is a trade-off that must be made judiciously.
replication can be used to improve the availability of a service, but only to the extent that the service is willing to trade consistency for availability.
replication can be used to improve availability, but the benefits are not always as great as they seem.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the benefits of replication for availability are not limited to high-availability scenarios; even in the face of infrequent failures, the availability gains are substantial.
availability is a first-order design constraint that should be considered early in service design.
the costs and limits of wide-area replication are significantly lower than commonly assumed.
